record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own CIFAR-10 training-error outcomes for several normalization variants, including a result where LayerNorm improves convergence but generalizes worse, and pRMSNorm has higher test error. These findings refine the normalization-related scope in V6; they do not test the main random-initialization, width, depth, or learning-rate claims.
record.gate_note: The CIFAR-10 section reports training error rates for the modified ConvPool-CNN-C model, so those outcomes qualify as rows for V6. The paper's translation and retrieval convergence results use different tasks and measures from the listed claim versions and are not catalog rows. The paper does not test V1, V2, V3, V4, or V5.
record.test_reason: The study reports BatchNorm accelerating convergence in new CNN and LSTM settings, bearing on V6. Its CIFAR-10 training-classification-error trajectories also bear on V1, although their endpoints cannot be read from the supplied text. LayerNorm and RMSNorm results alone do not test the BatchNorm claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record broadly captures the conclusion: RMSNorm can replace LayerNorm across the tested architectures with comparable quality and observed running-time reductions of 7–64%, depending on implementation and setting. The authors do not find consistent additional speed improvements from pRMSNorm. The CIFAR-10 summary is accurate qualitatively; its numerical differences should be stated as 0.13 percentage points better than baseline for RMSNorm and 1.54 points worse than RMSNorm for pRMSNorm.
record.recipe_differences: The paper compares normalization choices in a modified ConvPool-CNN-C classification model; it does not reproduce the same experiments or methods described in the claim versions.
record.method_sensitivity: Normalization choice changes CIFAR-10 test error; learning rate differs between Baseline (0.0003) and normalization variants (0.003).

fits_no_version.finding: LayerNorm, RMSNorm and pRMSNorm have CIFAR-10 test errors of 10.49%, 8.83% and 10.37%, versus 8.96% without normalization.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Normalization variants differ in final generalization performance on the modified ConvPool-CNN-C.

fits_no_version.finding: RMSNorm generally matches LayerNorm quality while reducing computation time; LayerNorm and RMSNorm also accelerate convergence on several tasks.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Removing mean centering from layer normalization can preserve its optimization benefits while reducing computational overhead.

record.problems: Table 9 training-error numbers are not legible in the supplied text, so the training-error outcomes cannot be independently assigned by model. The study uses a modified ConvPool-CNN-C and reports no uncertainty for CIFAR-10 error rates. The prose's stated RMSNorm improvement of 0.013% does not match the Table 10 values 8.96% and 8.83%.
record.rows_left_out: No legible training-error numbers can be extracted from Table 9; rows R1–R3 record the reported measure without reconstructing values. Translation and retrieval task outcomes were omitted because their metrics do not measure a behavior named by the versions.

untested.parts: Random or corrupted labels, CIFAR-100, systematic model-size comparisons, early stopping and regularization comparisons; readable evidence establishing near-zero training error is unavailable.
Teacher-student ReLU local minima and additional student neurons.
Depth-dependent degradation, identity shortcuts, deep plain tanh initialization and Fixup.

Activation-matched initialization, signal and gradient propagation, trainable depth, and orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization. The shifted-initialization experiment compares normalization methods rather than these claims.
Learning-rate stability thresholds, catapult dynamics, sharpness and edge-of-stability training.

Comparative learning-rate tolerance, Fixup, and the original MNIST, VGG and Inception settings. Using a higher learning rate for normalized CIFAR models does not independently establish greater tolerance.

missing.what: BatchNorm versus unnormalized CIFAR-10 training-error convergence: the text reports faster convergence and the best convergence among normalization variants. Include the different learning rates, 0.003 versus 0.0003, and distinguish epochs from wall-clock time.
missing.locator: Section 6.4, training-error plot captioned Table 9, Appendix A.4

missing.what: Separate BatchNorm-LSTM and BatchNorm-Everywhere validation-error trajectories against the unnormalized attentive-reader baseline. Both accelerate convergence; numerical curve values are unavailable in the supplied text.
The unnormalized, BatchNorm and WeightNorm CIFAR-10 training-error trajectories are omitted. They bear on training-error attainment, but their endpoints cannot be recovered from the supplied text.

record.verdict_notes: Remove the record's V6 limits_scope and challenges verdicts: final test errors for other normalization methods do not contradict a claim about BatchNorm accelerating training. No V1 verdict is justified without readable training-error outcomes. Neither tested version lists this study as an original source.

versions.untested_parts: Training classification error under SGD or Adam on CIFAR-10/CIFAR-100, random or corrupted labels, and effects of model size or training duration.
Two-layer ReLU teacher-student local minima and student width relative to teacher width.
Plain versus residual network depth effects, shortcuts, special deep tanh initialization, and Fixup training without normalization.
Activation-matched initialization, depth, orthogonal versus Gaussian initialization, and 10,000-layer convolutional training.
Training behavior above or near learning-rate stability limits and sharpness.

The listed sigmoid MNIST, VGG CIFAR-10, and Inception ImageNet speed and learning-rate-tolerance comparisons are not tested. The paper evaluates normalization variants on a modified ConvPool-CNN-C on CIFAR-10, including reported training error, but does not report speed as accuracy gain or learning-rate tolerance for those results.
